topics.title: Introduction to Monitoring and Evaluation
topics.description: An introduction to the basic concepts of Monitoring and Evaluation, why programmes undertake M&E, and how routine data collection and reporting support programme monitoring and performance assessment.
keyPoints: Monitoring is a continuous process involving the systematic collection and analysis of data to track the progress of a project or programme against its objectives.
Evaluation is a systematic process of assessing the relevance, effectiveness, efficiency and impact of activities to determine whether the project's goals have been achieved.
Monitoring and Evaluation involves systematically collecting, analysing and using data to track and assess programme performance and inform decisions.
Monitoring helps programmes follow implementation progress against established objectives.
Evaluation examines programme activities and their results to determine whether intended goals have been achieved.
The presentation introduces the results chain as a framework within M&E.
Routine M&E tools are used to track, report and analyse information about services provided by healthcare workers.
The training expects participants to understand key M&E concepts, why M&E is undertaken and the basics of data collection and reporting tools.
subtopics: Basic concepts and definitions of Monitoring and Evaluation
Reasons for undertaking Monitoring and Evaluation

topics.title: Data Collection and Reporting Tools
topics.description: An introduction to routine Monitoring and Evaluation tools used to collect, document, report and analyse information about healthcare services. The session explains the differences between cards, forms, registers and monthly summary forms, including their purposes and frequencies of use.
keyPoints: Routine M&E tools are used for tracking, reporting and analysing information on routine services provided by healthcare service providers.
Harmonised and standardised tools promote consistency in healthcare data collection and reporting.
Data collection and reporting tools may be maintained in paper or electronic formats.
Cards contain information about only one individual and typically capture information during one encounter. The presentation identifies their frequency of use as once.

Forms are data collection tools containing information about one individual. They are commonly used to collect information during an encounter and may be soft-bound booklets containing multiple sheets. Their frequency of use is daily.
Forms provide information that is transferred into registers.
Registers contain individual client records arranged in multiple rows. Each row represents one individual, while standard data elements are recorded in columns.
Registers are commonly completed daily and provide information for monthly summary forms.
Monthly Summary Forms are reporting tools that summarise and aggregate relevant information about services provided.
Monthly Summary Forms do not collect individual client information and are completed monthly.

topics.title: HIV Testing Services (HTS) Monitoring and Evaluation Tools
topics.description: An introduction to the harmonised HIV Testing Services monitoring and evaluation tools, their objectives and their role in documenting HIV testing activities, client information, service outcomes and programme reporting.
keyPoints: The HTS monitoring and evaluation tools support the documentation, monitoring and reporting of HIV Testing Services.
The training introduces four harmonised HTS tools.
HTS 001 is the HIV Testing Services Form. It provides baseline client information and documents pre-test counselling, risk assessment, diagnostic testing and service outcomes.

HTS 002 is the HIV Testing Services Register. It documents information about clients who receive HTS and other related tests, provides a summary of services delivered at service delivery points and serves as a source document for reporting.
HTS 003 is the Index Contact Testing Form. It combines elements of Family Index Testing, Partner Notification Service and index testing registration.
The HTS 003 form is used to enumerate and track sexual, biological and social contacts of an index client for HIV testing and linkage to treatment and OVC programmes.
HTS 004 is the HIV Testing Services Monthly Summary Form. It summarises and reports HTS and other relevant testing activities at facility level and supports reporting to higher programme levels.
The presentation outlines an HTS service flow that includes pre-test counselling and risk assessment, HIV testing, syphilis testing and post-test counselling.
The service flow includes result disclosure, confirmatory testing where required, recency testing and referrals to appropriate services.
Eligible HIV-negative clients may be referred for PrEP services, while clients with confirmed HIV-positive results are referred for ART.
Other referrals shown in the service flow include STI management, TB services and further assessment of suspected acute HIV infection.

topics.title: HTS Tools: Sections, Components and Completion
topics.description: A practical examination of the sections, data elements and completion procedures of the four harmonised HTS tools. The session explains the information recorded, who completes each tool, when it is completed, its information sources and where completed records should be kept.
keyPoints: The HTS 001 form is divided into facility identification, patient demographics, pre-test information, diagnostic testing, post-test counselling, comments and attestation.
Facility identification captures the State, LGA, facility name, service setting, date of visit and testing modality.
Client demographic information includes name, age, sex, marital status, client code, telephone number, address and other relevant client details.
Pre-test information includes client knowledge assessment, personal HIV risk assessment, clinical TB screening, syndromic STI screening and sex partner risk assessment.
The diagnostic testing section documents HIV test results, confirmatory HIV test results where applicable, syphilis results and recency results.
Post-test counselling documentation includes previous HIV testing information, result receipt, HIV self-test kits, index testing and relevant prevention services.
The HTS form must include the name, designation, signature and date of the healthcare worker or designated staff who completed it.
The HTS 002 register documents client identification, service delivery information, testing outcomes, referrals and other relevant programme data.
A new month should begin on a new page of the HTS register, and client serial numbering starts again from 0001 at the beginning of each new month.
The HTS 003 form has sections for site and index client information as well as the enumeration, notification, testing and linkage details of contacts.
The HTS 004 Monthly Summary Form has three parts: the head for facility identification, the body for aggregated HTS service information and the tail for authentication.
The HTS Monthly Summary Form uses register information as a source for calculating and reporting service totals.
The presentation identifies counsellors, HTS focal persons and other service providers providing HTS as personnel who complete the HTS form and register.
Completed forms and registers must be kept in appropriate secure locations accessible only to authorised personnel.

topics.title: PrEP and PEP Monitoring Tools
topics.description: An introduction to the revised Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis and Post-Exposure Prophylaxis monitoring tools. The session explains how the screening and eligibility form, PrEP and PEP card, register and monthly summary form support client assessment, service documentation, follow-up and programme monitoring.
keyPoints: The training aims to familiarise participants with the revised PrEP and PEP tools, explain their role in HIV prevention programme monitoring and improve accurate recording of client-level and aggregate data.
The PrEP and PEP Screening and Eligibility Form captures client information, HIV and STI risk assessment and other eligibility parameters.
The screening form also captures reasons why clients decline PrEP or PEP and is designed for use across multiple target populations.
The screening and eligibility form is completed by counsellor testers at every client encounter.
Its sections include demographics, pre-test counselling and risk assessment, HIV testing and PrEP eligibility.
The PrEP and PEP Card captures information about each client enrolled in PrEP or PEP and tracks services provided at each clinical visit.
The card contains front, centre and back pages. The front page includes demographics, PrEP or PEP initiation and completion, discontinuation or interruption information.
The centre page documents follow-up visits and the client's status at each clinical encounter.
The back page contains PEP follow-up information, including exposure details and follow-up HIV test results.
The card is completed at each clinical encounter by the relevant personnel, including medical records staff, data clerks, ART physicians, ART nurses or tracking teams.
The PrEP and PEP Register documents client information and programme interventions and supports cohort analysis and monthly reporting.
The register includes facility details, registration and personal information, PrEP initiation and follow-up, PEP documentation, discontinuation and ART linkage.
The register is completed by the healthcare worker providing PrEP and PEP services at the completion of each clinic day.
The PrEP and PEP Monthly Summary Form aggregates information about eligibility, initiation, follow-up, PrEP service delivery and PEP initiation.
The monthly summary form is completed at the end of each reporting month using information from the screening and eligibility form and the PrEP and PEP registers.
The presentation emphasises safe storage of the tools in secure cabinets or appropriate facility records locations.

topics.title: STI Monitoring and Reporting Tools
topics.description: An introduction to the Sexually Transmitted Infections Register and STI Monthly Summary Form. The session explains how STI screening, symptoms, syndromic assessment, diagnosis, aetiology, treatment and referrals are documented and reported.
keyPoints: The STI Register captures information about STI screening, symptoms, aetiology and HIV status.
The register collects client-level information and can be used to aggregate data and support cohort analysis.
The STI Register provides data required to complete the STI Monthly Summary Form.
The STI Register is divided into three sections: the header section, client registration section and STI management section.
The header records the month, year, facility name, State and LGA.
The client registration section documents personal information, which may be populated from the HTS or screening form.
The STI management section records relevant screening, testing and management information, including syndromic screening and aetiology.
The STI Register is completed by the healthcare worker providing STI services at the end of each clinic day.
The register is kept where STI services are provided and should be stored securely in a cabinet or file locker.
The STI Monthly Summary Form is a standardised reporting tool that summarises the delivery and uptake of STI services at facility level.
The STI Monthly Summary Form aggregates client-level information on syndromic screening, diagnosis and management across target populations.
The STI Monthly Summary Form is completed monthly by medical records personnel or data clerks.
The STI Register is the source of information for completing the STI Monthly Summary Form.

The presentation identifies four reporting areas: individuals screened for STI, individuals with an STI syndrome, individuals diagnosed with STI and individuals treated or referred for STI management.
Reported information is disaggregated by relevant characteristics, including target population, age, sex, syndrome, aetiology and outcome, as applicable to each indicator.
subtopics: Introduction to STI monitoring and reporting

topics.title: Viral Hepatitis Patient Monitoring Tools
topics.description: An introduction to the patient management and monitoring tools used in viral hepatitis services. The session covers the purpose of patient monitoring tools, data collection errors, the Viral Hepatitis Enrollment and Follow-up Card, the Viral Hepatitis Follow-up Card and the Viral Hepatitis Treatment Register.
keyPoints: Patient management and monitoring tools are designed to ensure follow-up of every patient.
The tools provide standardised instruments for capturing core patient information, including clinical records at different service delivery points.
Patient-level information provides a data source for aggregation into programme monitoring and evaluation.
The presentation identifies physical data collection errors, including illegible and missing entries.
Logic errors are identified by reviewing entries across a row to determine whether the information is logically consistent.
Examples of logic errors include duplicate numbers and recording a client as a TB patient while also documenting a TB screening score that is inconsistent with that classification.
Data errors should be reviewed by supervisory staff through routine register and logbook checks.
When an error is identified, the entire row should be reviewed to identify other possible errors or solutions.
Designated personnel should be responsible for documenting data errors and corrections.
Ongoing staff training helps address data problems and prevent recurring errors.
Registers and forms should be completed by designated staff and stored securely to protect confidentiality.
The Viral Hepatitis Enrollment and Follow-up Card captures baseline client information, clinical and laboratory evaluation, service provision and outcomes.
Its sections include header and demographics, screening, diagnosis, ancillary testing and clinical parameters, hepatitis B treatment, hepatitis C treatment, codes and follow-up information.
The card uses information from the client and laboratory reports and is completed by the attending clinician.

The Viral Hepatitis Follow-up Card tracks the progress of hepatitis B treatment through visit dates, vital signs, HBV tests, liver function tests, staging, treatment regimen, next appointment and outcomes.
The Viral Hepatitis Treatment Register tracks hepatitis B and C treatment, co-infections, drugs used, treatment duration, monitoring and treatment outcomes.
The treatment register includes header and demographics, HBV screening and diagnosis, HCV screening and diagnosis, HBV treatment and HCV treatment.
Monitoring information includes relevant laboratory results, liver function and staging information, treatment regimens, follow-up dates and outcomes.
HCV treatment monitoring includes treatment duration, treatment completion, HCV RNA testing, sustained virological response assessment and retreatment information where applicable.
Patient monitoring records should be maintained in the appropriate client folder or secure records location accessible only to authorised personnel.

topics.title: Data Quality, Error Correction and Confidentiality
topics.description: Understanding data collection errors and the procedures presented for identifying, correcting and preventing them. The session also explains the responsibilities of designated staff and the importance of secure storage and confidentiality when handling healthcare records.
keyPoints: Data collection errors can affect the accuracy and reliability of healthcare records and programme monitoring information.
The presentation groups data collection errors into physical errors and logic errors.
Physical errors include illegible entries and missing entries.
Logic errors are identified by reviewing information across an entire row in a register or form to check whether entries are logically consistent.
Examples of logic errors include duplicate numbers and inconsistencies between a client's TB classification and the recorded TB screening score.
Supervisory staff should be identified to review registers and audit logbooks daily and identify errors.
When an error is identified, staff should examine the entire row to identify other possible errors or appropriate solutions.
A designated person or group should be responsible for documenting data errors and corrections.
Staff should be informed about data error problems and receive ongoing training to prevent recurrence.
Registers and forms should be completed only by designated staff.
Registers and forms should be stored in secure locations to help maintain confidentiality.
The presentation also emphasises that completed HTS, PrEP, PEP, STI and viral hepatitis records should be accessible only to authorised personnel.
Accurate and properly maintained records support reliable programme monitoring and reporting.
subtopics: Duplicate numbers and other register errors
Daily register and audit logbook review
Ongoing staff training and supportive supervision

topics.title: Viral Hepatitis Monthly Summary and Reporting
topics.description: An introduction to the Viral Hepatitis Monthly Summary Form for hepatitis B and C services. The session explains its purpose, data sources, reporting process and the movement of aggregated facility information through LGA, State and National reporting levels.
keyPoints: The Viral Hepatitis Monthly Summary Form summarises and reports the required data elements and indicators for viral hepatitis services each month.
At facility level, the form provides an overview of daily and scheduled viral hepatitis activities carried out during the reporting month.
The form provides a current tally or summary of viral hepatitis services completed at facility and community service delivery points.
Facility services may include services provided at public or private facilities, while community services include outreach stations and mobile clinics.
Information from the Viral Hepatitis Laboratory and Treatment Registers is used to complete the monthly summary forms.
The training aims to familiarise participants with the VH Monthly Summary Form, improve accurate completion, identify data sources and explain the reported indicators.
The form is used at facility level to summarise services and at LGA, State and National levels to collate and report programme information.
At the end of the month, facility-level reports are submitted to the LGA level for compilation.
The LGA M&E officer compiles facility reports into an LGA report.
The State M&E officer receives and collates reports from LGAs into a State report.
The State report is then submitted to the National level.
The training emphasises identifying the correct source of information for each reported variable.
Participants are expected to accurately complete the VH Monthly Summary Form and explain the indicators reported.
The presentation also emphasises appropriate handling and safeguarding of the confidentiality of the monthly summary form.
The training includes group work to practise completion and understanding of the reporting tool.

topics.title: Practical Exercises and Group Work
topics.description: Applying the concepts and procedures covered during the training through practical exercises, client scenarios, monitoring tool completion, data review and group discussions. The presentation uses HTS, PrEP, PEP and viral hepatitis scenarios to reinforce correct documentation and reporting.
keyPoints: Practical exercises allow participants to apply M&E concepts and use the relevant routine healthcare documentation tools.
The presentation includes an HTS case scenario involving a couple attending a facility for HIV testing, with different previous testing histories and clinical information.
Participants are asked to identify and complete the necessary HTS tools for the clients described in the scenario.
The HTS exercise includes documentation of HIV testing outcomes, recency testing, index testing and HIV self-testing kits provided for children.
PrEP and PEP scenarios are used to practise completing screening and eligibility, initiation and follow-up documentation.
Participants are expected to identify the appropriate information to record during PrEP and PEP encounters.
STI exercises reinforce the documentation of screening, syndromic information, diagnosis, treatment and referral.
Viral hepatitis exercises allow participants to practise using patient monitoring and treatment documentation tools.
Group work is used to practise completing the Viral Hepatitis Monthly Summary Form and identifying the appropriate data sources for reported variables.
Data quality exercises help participants identify missing, illegible, duplicate and logically inconsistent entries.
Participants practise reviewing records and identifying possible errors and corrections.
The training uses a parking-lot approach in which participants write down areas they do not understand so that these can be addressed at the end of the presentation.
Participants are expected to use the relevant user guides and instructions when completing the monitoring tools.
The exercises reinforce accurate documentation, appropriate reporting, secure storage and confidentiality.
